tagline.text: The world's only organ still played on bamboo pipes, sounding for 200 years

image.credit: Ralff Nestor Nacor / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

items.credit: Eugene Alvin Villar (seav) / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons
Ervin Malicdem / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: Built of bamboo by a Spanish priest, Fr. Diego Cera, in the early 19th century, this is the world's only bamboo pipe organ still played today, and it's a National Cultural Treasure. You can hear the organ's sound in person at the stone-built St. Joseph Parish Church, and see the story of its 200-year restoration at a small museum.

The Las Piñas Bamboo Organ is a pipe organ set in the choir loft of St. Joseph Parish Church, at the southern edge of Metro Manila in Las Piñas City. The church and organ were built by Fr. Diego Cera, a Spanish Recollect missionary who arrived as the first parish priest of Las Piñas around
, built the stone church, and then began building the organ in
, completing it in the
early 1820s

The organ has 1,031 pipes, of which 902 are made of bamboo — only the horizontal trumpet-toned pipes are metal. With metal pipe material hard to import from Europe, Fr. Cera is said to have chosen bamboo, plentiful in the Philippines, and finished the instrument with local techniques such as burying the bamboo in salty sand to keep out insects. The soft, warm tone unique to bamboo is what gives this organ its character.
After the church and organ were badly damaged by an earthquake in
and a typhoon in

, it went for a long time without being properly played. In the 20th century, a restoration movement took hold: the whole organ was sent to the Klais organ workshop in Bonn, Germany, for a major restoration in
, and it returned to Las Piñas to sound again in
March 1975
. It was declared a National Cultural Treasure in
, and local organ craftsmen completed a second round of maintenance around the same time.

Though modest in scale, it's a special experience for music-loving travelers and anyone interested in the Philippines' colonial-era churches and craftsmanship. Being close to the airport, it fits neatly into a half day on your first day in Manila or before departure, and every February, during the International Bamboo Organ Festival, you can hear performances by organists from around the world.

Book a museum guided tour and you'll often get a short organ performance included. The low, soft resonance the bamboo pipes produce is distinctly different from a metal organ. Confirm whether a performance is included when you book the tour.

blocks.title: A close look from the choir loft

children.text: The guided tour takes you up to the choir loft on the second floor, showing the pipes, keyboard, and wood carvings up close. Seeing the bamboo joints still visible on the pipes up close makes clear this is a hand-built instrument.

In the museum, housed in the former convent building next to the church, you can see the life of Fr. Diego Cera, the German restoration process, and the old pipes and parts that were replaced. It's small, so 30 minutes to an hour is enough.

blocks.title: The stone-built St. Joseph Parish Church

children.text: A modest colonial-era church built of stacked volcanic stone, with a low bell tower, thick walls, and a dark wooden ceiling that suit the organ well. The plaza in front of the church and its old-style lampposts are good for photos.
The organ is often used to accompany Sunday Mass, especially the evening Mass. Hearing it ring out alongside the hymns makes clear that this instrument is a living one, not just a museum piece.
Held every
February
since
, this classical music festival features performances by organists from abroad along with the Las Piñas Boys Choir and an orchestra. In
, the 52nd festival is scheduled for

During the nine-day Christmas novena Masses held each dawn from
December 16–24

, the church is decorated with lanterns and ornaments, and the organ and hymns together create a special atmosphere. Bibingka (rice cake) and puto bumbong sold outside the church after Mass are also worth trying.

Enter "Las Piñas Bamboo Organ" or "St. Joseph Parish Church Las Piñas" as your destination. The church stands in the old town center, at the corner of Quirino Avenue and Diego Cera Avenue.
Get off at Dr. Santos station, the southern end of the LRT-1 Cavite extension, and switch to a Grab or jeepney for about
15–30 minutes
. From downtown Manila, the LRT fare is about

From Baclaran or PITX (the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange), take a jeepney marked "Zapote" and get off near Las Piñas church. The fare is about
, and travel time runs
30 minutes–1 hour
depending on traffic. Just tell the driver to let you off at "Bamboo Organ."

From Manila, head south along Roxas Boulevard and take CAVITEX toward Zapote. The streets around the church are narrow with little parking, so if the church lot is full, use a nearby paid parking area.
Since the visit is mostly indoors, it doesn't vary much by season, but the
December–April
dry season is best for getting around.
February

in particular brings the International Bamboo Organ Festival, with performances every evening. Popular shows sell out early, so check the schedule and tickets in advance on the official website and Facebook page.
During the
June–October

rainy season, low-lying roads in Las Piñas and Parañaque flood easily, and traffic backs up badly when a typhoon hits. Bamboo is sensitive to changes in humidity, so performances may be limited depending on the organ's condition. In
December
, the church looks its most beautiful with the dawn Masses and decorations of the Christmas season, and church events are also held around the
March 19
Feast of St. Joseph.

Las Piñas is a residential city, so there aren't many traveler-oriented hotels. Staying in Entertainment City, the casino-resort district in nearby Parañaque, or a hotel around Pasay's Mall of Asia (about
per night), makes it easy to combine the organ visit with airport transfers. For something cheaper, there are also business hotels in Parañaque and Las Piñas (about

Las Piñas is known as a town that once dried seawater to make salt, and seafood restaurants line the Manila Bay coast. Around the church there are restaurants serving Filipino home cooking and bakeries, and a short drive away, the Alabang–Zapote Road and Daang Hari area has large malls and restaurant clusters. Nearby, dampa-style seafood market restaurants along the Parañaque coast road cook the fish and shrimp you buy on the spot, making a good lunch or dinner stop after visiting the organ.
Guided tours and short performances often run by reservation. Contact the Bamboo Organ Foundation by email or Facebook in advance with your date and party size.
The museum generally operates on weekdays roughly from
10 AM to 5 PM
, but hours change often. Check the latest notices on the
Bamboo Organ Foundation official website
before your visit.
Choir loft tours pause during Masses and weddings. Weekday mornings are less crowded than weekends.
The choir loft stairs are narrow and steep. Wear comfortable shoes and leave large bags downstairs before climbing.
To really hear the organ's sound, sitting in the pews in the middle of the church, rather than in the choir loft, gives better resonance.
Being close to the airport, if you have an afternoon flight on your departure day, you can visit in the morning and head straight to the airport. Allow extra time for traffic.

To ask about guided tours and mini-concert bookings, contact the Bamboo Organ Foundation office (email bambooorganoffice@gmail.com, phone 02-8825-7190). If you're in a group, get in touch well ahead of your preferred date.

The bamboo organ is a cultural treasure highly sensitive to humidity and temperature. Never touch the pipes or keyboard, and follow your guide's directions while in the choir loft. Performances or choir loft viewings may be suspended during maintenance.
Refrain from flash photography and walking around during Mass.
The Alabang–Zapote Road and the CAVITEX ramp leading into Las Piñas get very congested during rush hour. Allow plenty of travel time.
Low-lying roads around the church can flood during the rainy season, so postpone your visit if heavy rain is forecast.
Sidewalks around the church are narrow with heavy vehicle and tricycle traffic, so walk carefully.
